The '''knowledge economy''', or '''knowledge-based economy''', is an [[economic system]] in which the production of goods and services is primarily driven by [[Knowledge intensive services|knowledge-intensive activities]] that contribute to the advancement of [[Technology|technical]] and scientific [[innovation]].<ref name=":0" /> The key element of value in this paradigm lies in the increased reliance on [[human capital]] and [[intellectual property]] as primary sources of innovative [[idea]]s, [[information]], and [[Practice (learning method)|practices]]. Organizations are called upon to leverage this "knowledge" in their production processes to stimulate and consolidate their [[business development]]. This approach is characterized by reduced dependence on [[Factors of production|physical input]]s and [[natural resource]]s. A knowledge-based economy is founded on the crucial role of [[intangible asset]]s within organisations as an enabler of modern [[economic growth]].<ref name=":16">{{Cite book|last=World|first=Bank|title=Building Knowledge Economies: Advanced Strategies for Development|publisher=World Bank Publications|year=2007|isbn=9780821369579|location=H Street, NW,Washington, DC|pages=4–12}}</ref>

==Overview==

===Description===
A knowledge economy features a highly [[Skilled worker|skilled workforce]] within both [[Microeconomics|microeconomic]] and [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomic]] environment. Institutions and industries create employment opportunities that necessitate highly [[Skill|specialized skills]] to satisfy the demands of the [[Market (economics)|global market]].<ref name=":1" /> Knowledge is viewed as an additional [[Factors of production|input]] to [[Work (human activity)|labour]], and [[Capital (economics)|capital]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Commission|first=European|title=Conference on knowledge economy - Challenges for Measurement|publisher=Eurostat|year=2005|isbn=92-79-02207-5|location=Luxembourg: Office for Official Publications of the European Communities|pages=9–13}}</ref> In principle, an individual's primary [[individual capital|capital]] is constituted by knowledge, together with the ability to perform and to generate [[economic value]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite conference|last=Kwon|first=Dae-Bong|date=27–30 Oct 2009|title=Human capital and its measurement |conference=The 3rd OECD World Forum on "Statistics, Knowledge and Policy": Charting Progress, Building Visions, Improving Life|url=https://www.oecd.org/site/progresskorea/44109779.pdf|pages=1–15|publisher=[[OECD]]}}</ref>

In a knowledge economy, highly skilled jobs require excellent technical skills and [[social skills|relational skills]]<ref name="DusiMessetti2014">{{cite journal|last1=Dusi|first1=Paola|last2=Messetti|first2=Giuseppina|last3=Steinbach|first3=Marilyn|title=Skills, Attitudes, Relational Abilities & Reflexivity: Competences for a Multicultural Society|journal=Procedia - Social and Behavioral Sciences|volume=112|year=2014|pages=538–547|issn=1877-0428|doi=10.1016/j.sbspro.2014.01.1200|doi-access=free}}</ref> such as [[Problem solving|problem-solving]], the flexibility to interface with [[Interdisciplinarity|multiple discipline areas]] as well as the ability to adapt to changes as opposed to moving or [[craft]]ing [[physical object]]s in conventional [[Manufacturing|manufacturing-based economies]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Harpan|last2=Draghici|first1=Ioana|first2=Anca|date=20 Mar 2014|title=Debate on the Multilevel Model of the Human Capital Measurement|journal=Procedia - Social and Behavioral Sciences|volume=124|pages=170–177|doi=10.1016/j.sbspro.2014.02.474|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kofler |first1=Ingrid |last2=Innerhofer |first2=Elisa |last3=Marcher |first3=Anja |last4=Gruber |first4=Mirjam |last5=Pechlaner |first5=Harald |title=The Future of High-Skilled Workers: Regional Problems and Global Challenges |location=Cham, Switzerland |publisher=[[Springer Verlag]] |year=2020 |isbn=9783030428709 |pages=29–41}}</ref> A knowledge economy stands in contrast to an [[agrarian economy]], in which the primary economic activity is [[subsistence farming]] for which the main requirement is [[manual labour]]<ref>{{Cite web|last=Johnson|first=D. Gale|date=16 Jan 2019|title=Agricultural economics|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/agricultural-economics|access-date=16 Oct 2020|website=Encycloaedia Britannica, Inc.}}</ref> or an [[industrialized economy]] that features [[mass production]] in which most of the workers are relatively [[Unskilled labour|unskilled]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Wokutch|first=Richard E.|date=12 Feb 2014|title=Newly industrialized country|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/newly-industrialized-country|access-date=16 Oct 2020|website=Encycloaedia Britannica}}</ref>

A knowledge economy emphasizes the importance of skills in a [[service economy]], the third phase of economic development also called a [[post-industrial economy]]. It is related to an [[information economy]], which emphasizes the importance of information as non-physical capital, and a [[digital economy]], which emphasizes the degree to which [[information technology]] facilitates trade. For companies, intellectual property such as [[trade secret]]s, [[copyright]]ed material, and [[patent]]ed processes become more valuable in a knowledge economy than in earlier eras.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last1=Houghton|first1=John|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/10826008.pdf|title=A Primer on the Knowledge Economy|last2=Sheehan|first2=Peter|publisher=Centre for Strategic Economic Studies, Victoria University of Technology|year=2000|location=Melbourne City}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stehr|first1=Nico|last2=Mast|first2=Jason L.|title=Knowledge Economy|journal=Handbook on the Knowledge Economy, Volume Two|doi=10.4337/9781781005132.00009|isbn=9781781005132|year=2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Foundations of the knowledge economy: innovation, learning, and clusters|date=2012|publisher=Edward Elgar|others=Westeren, Knut Ingar.|isbn=978-0-85793-771-1|location=Cheltenham, UK|oclc=758983832}}</ref><ref name=":11">{{Cite book|last=Unger, Roberto Mangabeira|title=The knowledge economy|isbn=978-1-78873-497-4|location=London|oclc=1050279840|date=2019-03-19}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Citation|chapter=OECD Work on Knowledge and the Knowledge Economy|date=2006|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/advancingknowled0000unse|title=Advancing Knowledge and The Knowledge Economy|publisher=The MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-25645-2|access-date=2020-02-10|chapter-url-access=registration}}</ref>

The global economy's transition to a knowledge economy<ref>{{cite journal |first=Keith |last=Smith |year=2002 |title=What is the 'Knowledge Economy'? Knowledge Intensity and Distributed Knowledge Bases |journal=Discussion Papers from United Nations University, Institute for New Technologies, No. 6 |url=http://www.intech.unu.edu/publications/discussion-papers/2002-6.pdf |access-date=2013-09-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141228192257/http://www.intech.unu.edu/publications/discussion-papers/2002-6.pdf |archive-date=2014-12-28 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |chapter=Singapore's Transition to the Knowledge Economy: From Efficiency to Innovation |title=Knowledge, Productivity, and Innovation in Nigeria: Creating a New Economy |first1=Ismail |last1=Radwan |first2=Giulia |last2=Pellegrini |pages=145–161 |isbn=978-0-8213-8196-0 |year=2010 |location=Washington, DC |publisher=The World Bank |chapter-url=http://siteresources.worldbank.org/SOUTHASIAEXT/Resources/223546-1206318727118/4808502-1206318753312/slknowledgecase2.pdf }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |title=The Knowledge Economy |journal=[[Annual Review of Sociology]] |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=199–220 |year=2004 |doi=10.1146/annurev.soc.29.010202.100037 |first1=Walter W. |last1=Powell |first2=Kaisa |last2=Snellman }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Rothboeck |first=Sandra |year=2000 |title=Human Resources and Work Organization in the Knowledge Economy – The Case of the Indian Software Industry |url=http://www.eolss.net/Sample-Chapters/C15/E1-31-01-03.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://swopec.hhs.se/eijswp/papers/eijswp0156.pdf |title=Growth & Innovation Policies For a Knowledge Economy. Experiences From Finland, Sweden & Singapore |first1=Magnus |last1=Blomström |first2=Ari |last2=Kokko |first3=Fredrik |last3=Sjöholm |year=2002 |journal=Working Paper 156 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141222142438/http://swopec.hhs.se/eijswp/papers/eijswp0156.pdf |archive-date=2014-12-22 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=http://info.worldbank.org/etools/docs/library/252537/2009-12-18-142047_ADjeflat%20_Background_Report.pdf |title=Building Knowledge Economies for job creation, increased competitiveness, and balanced development |journal=Worldbank Draft |first=Pr. Abdelkader |last=Djeflat |year=2009 |archive-date=2019-10-28 |access-date=2013-02-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191028175900/http://info.worldbank.org/etools/docs/library/252537/2009-12-18-142047_ADjeflat%20_Background_Report.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Offshoring in a Knowledge Economy |first1=Pol |last1=Antràs |first2=Luis |last2=Garicano |first3=Esteban |last3=Rossi-Hansberg |year=2006 |journal=[[Quarterly Journal of Economics]] |volume=121 |issue=1 |pages=31–77 |doi=10.1093/qje/121.1.31 |url=http://dash.harvard.edu/bitstream/handle/1/3196323/antras_offshoring.pdf }}</ref> is also referred to as the [[Information Age]], bringing about an [[information society]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/economics/gii/gii_2012.pdf|year=2012 |title=The Global Innovation Index 2012: Stronger Innovation Linkages for Global Growth |editor-first=Soumitra |editor-last=Dutta |publisher=INSEAD |access-date=2025-06-18 }}</ref>
The term ''knowledge economy'' was made famous by [[Peter Drucker]] as the title of Chapter 12 in his book ''[[The Age of Discontinuity]]'' (1969), which Drucker attributed to economist [[Fritz Machlup]] in 1962, originating in the idea of [[scientific management]] developed by [[Frederick Winslow Taylor]].<ref name=":13">{{cite book |first=Peter |last=Drucker |year=1969 |title=The Age of Discontinuity; Guidelines to Our Changing Society |url=https://archive.org/details/ageofdiscontinui00druc |url-access=registration |publisher=Harper and Row |location=New York }}</ref>

=== Knowledge-based economy and human capital ===
In a knowledge economy, human intelligence is the key engine of economic development. It is an economy where members acquire, create, disseminate and apply knowledge to facilitate economic and social development.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last=Mikhailove, Kopylova|first=A.M, A.A.|date=15 Mar 2019|title=Interrelation of Information and Knowledge in the Economy of the Post-Industrial Society|url=https://www.shs-conferences.org/articles/shsconf/abs/2019/03/shsconf_pedtp2018_01003/shsconf_pedtp2018_01003.html|journal=Problems of Enterprise Development: Theory and Practice 2018|volume=62|pages=1003|via=SHS Web of Conferences}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kefela|first=Ghirmai T.|date=6 July 2020|title=Knowledge-based economy and society has become a vital commodity to countried|journal=International NGO Journal|volume=5|issue=7|pages=160–166|s2cid=32055689}}</ref>

An economic system that is not knowledge-based is considered to be inconceivable.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|last=Hudson|first=Ray|date=1 Sep 2007|title=From Knowledge-based Economy to … Knowledge-based Economy? Reflections on Changes in the Economy and Development Policies in the North East of England|url=http://dro.dur.ac.uk/5989/|journal=Regional Studies|volume=45|pages=991–1012|via=Taylor & Francis online journals}}</ref> It describes the process of [[Consumption (economics)|consumption]] and production activities that are satisfied from the application of workers' expertise - [[intellectual capital]] and typically represents a significant level of individual [[Economics|economic activities]] in modern [[Developed country|developed economies]] through building an interconnected and advanced global economy where sources of knowledge are the critical contributors.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last=Tufano, Valente, Graziano, Materazzo|first=Antonio, Roberto, Enza, Modestino|date=18 May 2018|title=Tech & knowledge-based economy: How mobile technologies influences the economics of small and medium activities.|url=http://www.toknowpress.net/ISBN/978-961-6914-23-9/MakeLearn2018.pdf|journal=Management, Knowledge and Learning International Conference 2018 - International School for Social and Business Studies|pages=1–65|isbn=978-961-6914-23-9|via=Toknowpress}}</ref>

The present concept of "knowledge" originates from the [[History|historical]] and [[Philosophy|philosophical]] studies by [[Gilbert Ryle]]<ref>{{Cite book|last=Ryle|first=Gilbert|title=The concept of mind|publisher=Abingdon : Routledge|year=1949|isbn=9780415485470|location=London|pages=92}}</ref> and [[Israel Scheffler]],<ref>{{Cite book|last=Scheffler|first=Israel|title=Conditions of knowledge: an introduction to epistemology and education.|publisher=Chicago : Scott, Foresman|year=1965|isbn=0226736687|location=Chicago|pages=92}}</ref> who conducted knowledge to the terms "[[procedural knowledge]]" and "[[Conceptual analysis|conceptual Knowledge]]" and identified two types of skills: "routine competencies or facilities" and "[[Critical thinking|critical skills]]" that is intelligent performance; and it's further elaborated by [[Bengt-Åke Lundvall|Lundvall]] and Johnson<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal|last1=Lundvall|first1=Bengt-äke|last2=Johnson|first2=Björn|date=Dec 1994|title=The Learning Economy|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13662719400000002|journal=Journal of Industry Studies|volume=1|issue=2|pages=23–42|doi=10.1080/13662719400000002|via=Taylor&Francis Online|url-access=subscription}}</ref> who defined "knowledge" as falling in four broad categories:

* ''Know-what'' refers to knowledge about facts. Like information, experts utilize know-what to fulfill their jobs, such as with complex occupations such as law and medicine.
* ''Know-why'' refers to scientific knowledge of [[principle]]s and [[Natural law|laws of motion]] in nature. It concerns the [[Research|theoretical research]] of scientific and [[Technology|technological]] fields, which is essential for allowing innovation in the [[Production (economics)|production process]] and products development in areas such as universities and specialized firms. It can also reduce error frequency in trial and error procedures.<ref name=":02" />
* ''Know-who'' refers to knowledge of specific and selective [[social relation]]s, identifying the key persons who know the solutions and can perform under difficult scenarios. Finding the right people can be more essential to innovation than simply knowing basic scientific knowledge.
* ''Know-how'' refers to practical skills which allow individuals to do different kinds of things. Individuals share experiences in groups with uniform practices. It constitutes the human capital of enterprises.

The [[World Bank]] has spoken of knowledge economies by associating it with a four-pillar framework that analyses the rationales of human capital-based economies:

* ''An educated and skilled [[labour force]]'' is required to establish a strong knowledge-based economy where workers continuously learn and apply their skills to build and practice knowledge efficiently.
* ''A dense and modern information infrastructure'' provides easy access to [[Information and communications technology|information and communication technology]] (ICT) resources to overcome the barrier of high [[transaction cost]]s and to facilitate the effectiveness in interacting, disseminating and processing the information and knowledge resources.
* ''An effective innovation system'' is needed to support a great level of innovation within firms, industries, and countries, allowing them to keep up with the latest global technology and human intelligence to utilize it for the domestic economy.
* ''Institutional regime that supports incentives for [[entrepreneurship]] and the use of knowledge'' suggests that an economic system should offer incentives for better efficiency in mobilizing and allocating resources and encourage entrepreneurship.

The advancement of a knowledge-based economy occurred when global economies promote changes in material production, together with the creation of rich mechanisms of economic theories after the Second World War that tend to integrate science, technology and the economy.<ref name=":12" />

[[Peter Drucker]] discussed the knowledge economy in the book ''The Effective Executive 1966'',<ref name=":13" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Drucker|first=Peter F.|date=2018-03-09|title=The Effective Executive|publisher=Routledge |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.4324/9780080549354|doi=10.4324/9780080549354|isbn=9780080549354}}</ref> where he described the difference between the manual workers and the knowledge workers. The manual worker is the one who works with their own hands and produces goods and services. In contrast, the knowledge worker works with their head rather than hands and produces ideas, knowledge, and information.

==Information versus knowledge==
Definitions around "knowledge" are considered to be vague in terms of the [[formal system|formalization]] and [[Scientific modelling|modeling]] of a knowledge economy, as it is rather a relative concept. For example, there is no sufficient evidence and consideration for whether the "[[information society]]" could serve or act as the "[[knowledge society]]" interchangeably. Information in general, is not equivalent to knowledge. Their use depends on the individual and group's preferences which are "economy-dependent".<ref>{{cite book|last=Flew|first=Terry|title=New Media: An Introduction|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2008|isbn=978-0-19-555149-5|edition=3rd|location=New York}}</ref> Information and knowledge together are production resources that can exist without interacting with other sources. Resources are highly independent of each other in the sense that if they connect with other available resources, they transfer into [[factors of production]] immediately, and production factors are present only to interact with other factors. Knowledge associated with [[Intellectual property|intellectual information]] then is said to be a production factor in the [[new economy]] that is distinguished from [[Factors of production|traditional production factors.]]<ref name=":5" />

==Evolution==
From the early days of economic studies, though economists recognised the essential link between knowledge and [[economic growth]], knowledge was still identified only as a supplemental element in economic factors. The idea behind it has transformed recently when new growth theory praised knowledge and technology in enhancing productivity and economic advancement.<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":14" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|last1=Švarc|first1=Jadranka|last2=Dabić|first2=Marina|date=2015-07-05|title=Evolution of the Knowledge Economy: a Historical Perspective with an Application to the Case of Europe|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s13132-015-0267-2|journal=Journal of the Knowledge Economy|volume=8|issue=1|pages=159–176|doi=10.1007/s13132-015-0267-2|s2cid=152957932|issn=1868-7865|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Kabir, Mitt Nowshade|title=Knowledge-based social entrepreneurship : understanding knowledge economy, innovation, and the future of social entrepreneurship|date=22 February 2019|isbn=978-1-137-34809-8|location=New York, NY|oclc=1089007311}}</ref>

=== Overview ===
The developed society has transitioned from an [[Agrarian society|agriculture-based economy]], that is, the [[Pre-industrial society|pre-industrial age]] where economy and wealth were primarily based upon agriculture, to an [[Industrial organization|industrial economy]] where the [[Secondary sector of the economy|manufacturing sector]] was booming. In the mid-1900s, world economies moved towards a [[Post-industrial society|post-industrial]] or [[mass production]] system, where they were driven by the service sector that creates greater wealth versus manufacturing; to the late 1900s - 2000s, knowledge economy emerged with the highlights of the power of knowledge and human capital sector, and it's now marked as the latest stage of development in global [[economic restructuring]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> In the final decades of 20th century, the knowledge economy became greatly associated with sectors based in [[Research-intensive cluster|research-intensive]] and [[High tech|high-technology industries]] as a result of the steadily increased demand for sophisticated [[Science|science-based]] innovations.<ref name=":12" /> The knowledge economy operates differently from the past as it has been identified by the upheavals (sometimes referred to as the '''knowledge revolution''') in technological innovations and the globally competitive need for differentiation with new [[goods and services]], and processes that develop from the research community (i.e., [[Research and development|R&D factors]], [[University|universities]], [[Laboratory|labs]], [[Education|educational institutes]]).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite book|last=Unger, Roberto Mangabeira|title=The knowledge economy|date=19 March 2019|isbn=978-1-78873-497-4|location=London|oclc=1050279840}}</ref> [[Thomas A. Stewart (journalist)|Thomas A. Stewart]] points out that just as the Industrial Revolution did not end agriculture because people have to eat, the Knowledge Revolution is unlikely to end manufacturing industries because of ongoing societal demands for physical goods and services.<ref>{{cite book|author=Stewart, Thomas A.|year=1997|title=Intellectual Capital|publisher=Bantam Doubleday Dell, New York|pages=17|isbn=978-0385483810}}</ref>

For the modern knowledge economies, especially in [[Developed country|developed countries]], information, and knowledge have always taken on enormous importance in the development of either traditional or industrial economies, particularly with the efficient use of [[factors of production]]. Owners of production factors should possess and master information and knowledge so as to apply them to economic activity.<ref name=":5" /> In the knowledge economy, the specialised [[Workforce|labor force]] is characterised as [[Computer literacy|computer literate]] and well-trained in handling data, developing [[algorithm]]s and simulated models, and innovating on processes and systems.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":15">{{Cite web|last=OECD|date=2001|title=COMPETENCIES FOR THE KNOWLEDGE ECONOMY|url=http://www.oecd.org/innovation/research/1842070.pdf|access-date=26 Oct 2020|website=OCED ORGANISATION FOR ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT}}</ref> Harvard Business School Professor [[Michael Porter]] asserts that today's economy is far more dynamic and that the conventional notion of [[comparative advantage]]s within a company has changed and is less relevant than the prevailing idea of [[competitive advantage]]s which rests on "making more productive use of inputs, which requires continual innovation".<ref name=":7">{{cite journal |first=Michael E. |last=Porter |title=Clusters and the New Economics of Competition |journal=[[Harvard Business Review]] |year=1998 |volume=December |issue= 6|pages=77–90 |url=http://isites.harvard.edu/fs/docs/icb.topic1188431.files/Class%2010%20Mar%205/GSD5421%20Porter%20New%20Economics%20of%20Competition%201998.pdf |pmid=10187248 }}{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Therefore, the technical [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] careers, including [[Computer science|computer scientists]], [[engineer]]s, [[chemist]]s, [[biologist]]s, [[mathematician]]s, and [[Scientist|scientific inventors]] will continue to see demand. Porter further argues that well-situated clusters (that is, [[Geographical cluster|geographic concentrations]] of interconnected companies and institutions in a particular field) are vital with global economies, connect locally and globally with linked [[Industry (economics)|industries]], [[Manufacturing|manufacturers]], and other entities that are related by skills, technologies, and other common inputs. Knowledge is the catalyst and connective tissue in modern economies.<ref name=":7" /> Ruggles and Holtshouse argue the change is characterised by a dispersion of power and by managers who lead by empowering [[knowledge worker]]s to contribute and make decisions.<ref>{{cite book|editor=Ruggles, Rudy and David Holtshouse|year=1999|title=The Knowledge Advantage|publisher=Capstone Business Books, Dover, NH|pages=49|isbn=978-1841120676}}</ref>

=== Green infrastructure ===
With Earth's depleting natural resources, the need for [[green infrastructure]], a logistics industry forced into [[Just in time (business)|just-in-time]] deliveries, growing global demand, regulatory policy governed by performance results, and a host of other items place a priority on knowledge, and research becomes paramount. Technical knowledge helps with problem-solving, measuring performance, and managing data. These skills are used to handle complex projects that involve different countries and different areas of study.<ref>{{cite book |author=The Brookings Institution |title=MetroPolicy: Shaping A New Federal Partnership for a Metropolitan Nation Report |year=2008 }}</ref>

=== Prevailing and future economic development ===
Prevailing and future economic development will be dominated by technology and network expansion, in particular on knowledge-based [[social entrepreneurship]] and [[entrepreneurship]] as a whole. The knowledge economy is incorporating the [[network economy]], where the relatively localised knowledge is being shared among and across various networks for the benefit of all network members, to gain [[economies of scale]] in a wider scale.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=The new development paradigm : education, knowledge economy and digital futures|others=Peters, Michael (Michael A.), 1948-, Besley, Tina, 1950-, Araya, Daniel, 1971-|isbn=978-1-4539-1136-5|location=New York, New York|oclc=876042578}}</ref><ref name=":3"/>

== Globalisation ==
The rapid [[Globalization|globalisation]] of economic activities is one of the main determinants of the emerging knowledge economy. While there are no doubts on the other stages of relative [[openness]] in the global economy, the prevailing pace and intensity of globalisation are without precedent.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":11" /> Fundamental [[Microeconomics|microeconomic]] forces are the significant drivers of globalizing economic activities and further demands for [[human intelligence]]. These forces include the rapid integration of the world's financial and capital markets since the early 1980s, which influences essentially each level of the [[developed country]]'s financial and economic systems; increased multinational origin of the inputs to productions of both [[goods and services]], technology transfers and information flow.<ref name=":16" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":14" /><ref name=":15" />

== Examples of knowledge economies ==
Worldwide examples congregate around regions or cities with high concentrations of talented human capital and are often accompanied with [[high tech]]-oriented companies as well as innovative [[tech hubs]].<ref>{{Cite web| title=Analysis of Investment in Knowledge inside OECD Countries | url=https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?repid=rep1&type=pdf&doi=9ccd5829007e152af91b3f21a8e20906b43b3e93 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240920045124/https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=9ccd5829007e152af91b3f21a8e20906b43b3e93&repid=rep1&type=pdf | archive-date=2024-09-20}}</ref> The knowledge economic hubs include information technology in [[Silicon Valley]], [[United States]]; water and agricultural technology in [[Silicon Wadi]], [[Israel]];<ref>Bay Area Economic Council, Sean Randolph, https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/SiliconValleyToSiliconWadi.pdf, October 2021</ref> aerospace and automotive engineering in [[Munich]], [[Germany]]; biotechnology in [[Hyderabad, India|Hyderabad]], [[India]]; electronics and digital media in [[Seoul]], [[South Korea]]; [[petrochemical]] and the renewable energy industry in [[Brazil]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Terra |first=Nana |title=Brazil is a world leader in renewable energy job creation |url=https://www.airswift.com/blog/renewable-energy-brazil |access-date=2024-07-02 |website=www.airswift.com |language=en}}</ref> Many other cities and regions try to follow a knowledge-driven development paradigm and increase their knowledge base by investing in higher education and research institutions to attract highly skilled labour and better position themselves in the global competition.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Koukoufikis|first1=Giorgos|title=Building a knowledge-driven city The case of the Gran Sasso Science Institute in L 'Aquila, Italy|url=https://www.academia.edu/22442110|access-date=3 March 2016}}{{Dead link|date=April 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Yet, despite digital tools democratising access to knowledge, research shows that knowledge economy activities remain as concentrated as ever in traditional economic cores.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ojanperä|first1=Sanna|last2=Graham|first2=Mark|last3=Straumann|first3=Ralph|last4=Sabbata|first4=Stefano De|last5=Zook|first5=Matthew|date=2017-03-08|title=Engagement in the Knowledge Economy: Regional Patterns of Content Creation with a Focus on Sub-Saharan Africa|url=http://itidjournal.org/index.php/itid/article/view/1479|journal=Information Technologies & International Development|language=en|volume=13|pages=19|issn=1544-7529|access-date=2017-12-05|archive-date=2017-12-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171206074550/http://itidjournal.org/index.php/itid/article/view/1479|url-status=dead}}</ref><gallery mode="packed">

==Technology==
The technology requirements for a [[national innovation system]], as described by the [[World Bank Institute]], must be able to disseminate a [[unified process]] by which a working method may converge scientific and technology solutions and organizational solutions.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Tho, Q.T. |author2=Hui, S.C. |author3=Fong, A.C.M. |author4=Tru Hoang Cao |journal=IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering |title=Automatic Fuzzy Ontology Generation for Semantic Web |volume=18 |issue=6 |year=2006 |pages=842–856 |doi=10.1109/TKDE.2006.87 |s2cid=17557226 }}</ref> According to the World Bank Institute's definition, such [[innovation]] would further enable the World Bank Institute's vision outlined in its [[Millennium Development Goals]].

===Challenges for developing countries===
The United Nations Commission on Science and Technology for Development report (UNCSTD, 1997) concluded that for developing countries to integrate ICTs successfully and [[sustainable development]] to participate in the knowledge economy, they need to intervene collectively and strategically.<ref>{{cite book |author=UNCSTD |year=1997 |title=United Nations Commission on Science and Technology for Development |work=Report of the Working Group on ICTs for Development prepared for the 3rd Session |location=12 May, Geneva, Switzerland }}</ref> Suggested collective intervention includes the development of effective national ICT policies that support the new regulatory framework, promote the selected [[knowledge production]], and use of ICTs and harness their organizational changes to be in line with the [[Millennium Development Goals]]. The report further suggests that developing countries develop the required ICT strategies and policies for institutions and regulations, considering the need to be responsive to the issues of convergence.
